title: Research
text:
Working papers

Bayesian Treatment Imputation for CATE Estimation Under Missing Binary Treatments In preparation Lim, J. & Reiter, J. P.
A fully Bayesian data augmentation Gibbs sampler that jointly updates a BART outcome model, a probit propensity model, and partially missing binary treatments in a single chain, propagating the parameter uncertainty that sequential multiple imputation discards.


Bayesian Causal Inference: A Practical Guide In preparation Lim, J. & Li, F. · for the Journal of Statistical Software
Introduces BayesCausal, an R package for Bayesian estimation of average and heterogeneous treatment effects under unconfoundedness, instrumental variables, and panel designs behind a single formula interface, with Stan/HMC posterior inference.

title: Joshua Lim
text:
I’m a third year Ph.D. candidate in the Department of Statistical Science at Duke University, working with Jerry Reiter and Fan Li.
My research sits at the intersection of causal inference and missing data. Specifically, I seek to develop Bayesian methodology that can estimate heterogeneous treatment effects in the presence of missing data.
Before Duke I graduated summa cum laude from UCLA in 2024 with a B.S. in Applied Mathematics, Statistics and Data Science. Alongside my methods work I collaborate as a biostatistician with Duke, UC San Diego, and previously Stanford University Schools of Medicine.
I am highly passionate about teaching. In Summer 2026 I was instructor of record for STA 199L: Introduction to Data Science and Statistical Thinking.
Outside the department you’ll find me on the court with Duke Men’s Club Volleyball, performing with Duke Chinese Dance, flipping with Duke Gymnastics, or loudly defending UCLA sports deep in ACC country.

section: Teaching things I’m not paid to teach
text:
Teaching things I’m not paid to teach
In 2021 I built a free asynchronous multivariable calculus course — 22 lectures, homework, quizzes, two midterms, three projects, and a final — because the students who most needed a head start were the least likely to be able to pay for one. Ten people took it that first summer, and new students still work through the material every year.
